opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I've thought about quite a lot, actually. In chess or competitive sports, success is very clearly defined. There's a rating, there's a ranking, there's a scoreboard. You win or you lose. And the rules of the game are fixed. Everyone is playing the same game, and the only question is who plays it better.

Research is fundamentally different, because the most important part of research is that you get to define the game yourself. Of course there are benchmarks, leaderboards, citation counts, best paper awards, and in our field, especially in AI, people can get very caught up in those. You can treat research like a competitive sport: someone publishes a number, you beat it by 0.5%, you publish, then someone beats you. That's a kind of success, but I think it's a pretty shallow one, and it doesn't last very long. Those numbers get overwritten in a few months.

For me, success in research is more about whether you asked the right question at the right time, and whether what you did changed how other people think. Sometimes the most influential work isn't the one that wins on a benchmark. It's the one that opens a new direction, or simplifies something so much that people say, "Oh, of course, that's how it should be done." Sometimes it's even a negative result, showing that something everyone believed isn't really necessary. That kind of contribution is very hard to measure in the moment. Its value often only becomes clear years later.

Another difference is time scale. A chess game ends, and a season ends. Research doesn't really have an ending. You're never done. So if you define success too narrowly, as getting this paper accepted or winning this comparison, you'll burn out, because there's always another deadline and another competitor. I try to think of it more as a long game where taste matters a lot: developing a sense of what's important, what's beautiful, what will still matter in five or ten years.

And finally, research is much less zero-sum. In chess, if I win, you lose. In research, if someone else solves a problem I care about, the field still moves forward, and I can build on it. The best researchers I know are very competitive, but they also genuinely enjoy other people's good ideas. So I'd say success in research is less about winning and more about contributing something real and durable, and keeping your curiosity alive while doing it.

r001.rationale: The response describes success as making a real, durable contribution, but does not claim that one successful contribution alone can make a research career successful.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, actually, because I grew up in China where competition was everywhere, and for a long time I did carry that mindset into research without really noticing.

In chess or in sports, success has a very clean definition. There's a board, there's a clock, there's a scoreboard. You win or you lose, and everyone agrees on what happened. The feedback is immediate and the metric is shared by the entire community. If you beat Magnus Carlsen, nobody debates whether that counts.

Research doesn't work like that, even though people try very hard to make it look like it does. We have leaderboards, we have benchmarks, we have citation counts, we have the number of papers at NeurIPS or CVPR. And when you're a student, those things feel exactly like a scoreboard. You see a lab put out ten papers and you think, I'm losing. I certainly felt that way early on.

But I've come to believe that the scoreboard in research is mostly an illusion, or at least it's measuring the wrong game. The real goal of research is to change how people think about a problem. Sometimes that happens with a paper that gets rejected, or with an idea that only matters five years later. ResNeXt, ConvNeXt, the diffusion transformer work, all of those were in some sense me asking "do we really need this?" rather than me trying to climb a leaderboard. The leaderboard numbers were a side effect of asking a good question, not the target.

Another big difference is that in sports the game is fixed. In research, the most valuable move is often to change the game itself. If you're always optimizing for the current benchmark, by definition you are following someone else's definition of the problem. The people I admire most are the ones who decided the benchmark was asking the wrong thing.

And finally, research is not zero-sum. In chess, my win is your loss. In research, when someone else makes progress, I benefit. Their work becomes my tool next year. So the competitive framing is actually counterproductive. It makes you secretive, it makes you rush, and it makes you choose safe problems where you can guarantee a result.

So if I had to summarize, in competitive sports success is about being better than others at a well-defined task. In research, success is about being right about something that matters before it's obvious, and then being generous enough that others can build on it. The first one you can see on a scoreboard. The second one you often only know in hindsight, and you have to be comfortable living with that uncertainty for a long time. That's the hard part, and honestly I'm still learning it.

r001.rationale: The response describes research success as changing how people think and being right about something that matters, but it does not claim that one successful contribution can be enough to make a research career successful.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest difference is that in chess or competitive sports, the objective is relatively clear. You have rules, you have a score, and you know whether you won or lost. Research doesn’t really give you that kind of scoreboard. Part of the work is deciding what game is worth playing in the first place—what questions matter, and what would count as progress.

Of course, we have things that look like scores: papers, citations, awards. They provide feedback, but they’re imperfect measures of success. You can become very good at optimizing those measures without necessarily doing the work that will matter most in the long run. And sometimes an important idea takes years to be understood or useful.

So for me, success in research is more about whether you’ve helped people understand something they couldn’t understand before, or opened up a direction that other people can build on. There’s competition, certainly, but someone else succeeding doesn’t mean you’ve lost. Their discovery might make your next discovery possible. That makes research a very different kind of pursuit.

r001.rationale: The response describes research success as helping people understand something or opening a direction for others, but it does not claim that one successful contribution is enough to make a career successful.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is that in chess or competitive sports, the rules and the goal are relatively clear. You know what it means to win, and you have a ranking that tells you roughly where you stand. In research, you don’t really have that. Part of the work is deciding what game is worth playing in the first place.

You can measure papers, citations, awards, but those are imperfect signals. You might be very successful by those measures without doing the work that matters most to you. And a research direction can look unproductive for a long time before its value becomes clear.

So I would think about success less as beating other people and more as developing your own judgment: Can you identify an important question? Can you pursue it independently? Can you produce something that changes how people think or enables them to do something they couldn’t do before? There’s still competition, of course, but there isn’t one scoreboard that captures all of that.

r001.rationale: The response describes valuable research contributions, but it does not claim that one successful contribution can be enough to make a research career successful.
